title: Snow could shape winter air travel
copy: Flight bookings for this winter are running below recent seasons, with air service down 8% November through April compared to last year. Travelers are waiting on snowfall before committing to flights. Breeze's Orange County–Montrose route is paused, but United, American, Southwest, and Denver Airlines are all operating this winter.

title: Keeping warm on a frigid mountain
copy: Beacon Telluride is collecting gently used winter gear — jackets, gloves, base layers, hats, ski pants — for seasonal workers who may arrive underprepared for mountain cold. Drop-offs accepted at The Toggery through Nov. 15. The nonprofit also runs home-cooked meal hosting and other programs for seasonal employees all winter.

title: More flooding possible in Four Corners region after days of heavy rain
copy: Heavy rain since Wednesday has caused significant flooding across the Four Corners region, with rivers surging into homes and forcing evacuations — especially around Farmington, New Mexico. Saturated soils have a flood watch still in effect, with more storms expected. Officials warn returning residents of contaminated water, gas leaks, and other hazards.

title: Telluride Rewind
copy: Telluride's old town ordinances from 1966 included bans on opium dens, women loitering near saloons, and wearing clothing of the opposite sex. A 1981 council gave initial approval to convert the Nugget Theater into a 485-seat convention center. And in 1991, KOTO's Halloween bash drew 500-plus people and raised over $4,000.

title: Initial review of Shandoka parking structure approved by P&Z
copy: P&Z approved the preliminary PUD review for the Shandoka Lot Redevelopment, a proposed mixed-use project on the current surface parking lot that would include 50–60 housing units (80% deed-restricted affordable), a 900-vehicle parking structure, childcare, a food bank, and commercial space. The structure would replace 330 existing surface spots and absorb 288 spaces relocated from Carhenge. Some residents raised concerns about the added walking distance and traffic; HARC review continues Nov. 18.

title: Voters in 2 Democratic strongholds could ban transgender girls from girls school sports
copy: Voters in Colorado and Washington will decide ballot measures in 2026 to ban transgender girls from female school sports — the first time the question goes directly to voters rather than legislatures. Both states have Democratic-controlled governments that previously blocked such bans. Twenty-seven states already have these laws in place.

title: More rain is expected after bad flooding in the Four Corners region led to rescues and evacuations
copy: Severe flooding hit the Four Corners region this week, prompting 20 rescues, evacuations of 600 homes, and power outages for roughly 1,500 people in the Farmington and Shiprock areas. Four inches of rain fell on already-saturated ground Wednesday through Friday, with more expected. Southern Colorado saw flooding a full three feet above last year's 100-year flood level on the San Juan River.

title: Lottery for three-bedroom unit is open
copy: A deed-restricted 3-bed/2-bath condo at 226 East Pacific Avenue is up for lottery. Applications open Oct. 22 via SMRHA; submission window is Oct. 30–Nov. 20, with the drawing Dec. 11. Sale price is $453,000. Apply at smrha.org/applications — the window is short.

title: Chamberlain award winner Kingston featured at Bardic Trails
copy: Kate Kingston of Trinidad — a decorated Colorado poet with a long list of awards and fellowships — headlines Bardic Trails on Tuesday, Nov. 3 at 7 p.m. via Zoom. The free monthly series is hosted by Talking Gourds and open to all; the suggested prompt is "Dia de los Muertos." Visit tellurideinstitute.org/talking-gourds for the link.

title: A postcard from the Czech Republic
copy: Telluride High School sophomore Maddy Charleston is 11 months into a Rotary Youth Exchange in Jindřichův Hradec, Czech Republic — her first time traveling solo or outside the U.S. She's living with a host family, attending school, and picking up the language. The Telluride Rotary Club is also looking for a local family to host a Brazilian exchange student starting after the winter holidays.

title: Rooftop rescues and evacuations as severe flooding soaks Four Corners region
copy: Severe flooding hit the Four Corners region Friday, with rooftop rescues underway in San Juan County and some 600 Farmington households ordered to evacuate along the San Juan River. Southern Colorado saw flooding a full three feet above last year's 100-year flood event. More rain was forecast through the weekend.

title: 'We call it fellowship'
copy: AA meetings continue daily in Telluride at Christ Church, with a women's meeting resuming Thursdays at noon after an 18-month gap. Narcotics Anonymous meets Tuesdays at 5:30 p.m. Al-Anon recently ended its in-person run but online options remain via TellurideAlAnon@gmail.com.

title: Coffee and climate chats continue at the library
copy: A NOAA social scientist joins Sheep Mountain Alliance and EcoAction Partners Thursday, Oct. 29 at 8:30 a.m. at Wilkinson Public Library to talk about the anticipated "super El Niño" and what it might mean for the San Juans. The free Coffee & Climate Conversations series runs monthly. Tea, coffee, and pastries provided.

title: Here’s to your good health
copy: Uncompahgre Medical Center in Norwood is hosting a community forum Oct. 29, 6–8 p.m. at the Lone Cone Library to share plans for expanded primary care, at-home treatment, hospice services, and addiction medicine in the West End. UMC serves 66% of Norwood residents and ranks in the top 10% of Federally Qualified Health Centers nationally.

title: Expanding connections
copy: Lone Cone Library Director Kerry Bentler attended a rural libraries conference in Alabama on a scholarship from MacMillan Publishers, connecting with peers running operations closer to Norwood's scale. The library also has a new staff member, Daniella Pacheco-Rushing, and ongoing programs including a kids' STEAM series and weekly tech help sessions.

title: Spooky stagecraft
copy: Kindergarten through second-grade students from the Sheridan Arts Foundation's Young People's Theater will perform two Halloween-themed shows at the Sheridan Opera House on Oct. 28 at 5:15 p.m. — an adaptation of "The Little Ghost who was a Quilt" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." The Adventures in Acting program runs each spring and fall, enrolling more than 40 young students annually.

title: Agriculture secretary says agency is 'full-bore ahead' on Forest Service reorganization
copy: The Trump administration is pushing forward with a major Forest Service reorganization — moving headquarters to Salt Lake City, closing 23 research stations, and replacing regional offices with state offices — despite a federal judge's order halting the plan. The Forest Service workforce has already dropped roughly 16%, from 39,000 to 33,000 employees. The outcome is still in the courts.

title: Colorado, Utah communities flood as yet more moisture saturates US Southwest
copy: Heavy monsoon moisture hammered the Four Corners region Thursday — 80 homes and 50 RVs flooded in Hurricane, Utah, mandatory evacuations ordered along four rivers in southern Colorado including through Pagosa Springs, and Arizona saw multiple tornadoes the night before. Pagosa Springs officials expect crests a foot higher than last year's flood. NWS says the ground is saturated after three or four rounds of this pattern in recent weeks.

title: Sister of American held in Russia says he didn't know he was being released until he saw US flag
copy: Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher, was released from a Russian prison Wednesday after more than four years — he didn't know he was being freed until he saw a U.S. flag on the plane. His sister says he was starved and beaten during his imprisonment. He's expected to eventually settle in Colorado.

title: ‘Overjoyed just to get away’
copy: Little Pink Houses of Hope brought 12 breast-cancer families from across the country to Telluride for a weeklong retreat — the second year running. Fifteen local sponsors covered lodging, food, and activities, from wagon rides at Schmid Family Ranch on Wilson Mesa to a rainy-day Jeep trip to Bridal Veil Falls. For families like one from Houston whose kids had never left Texas, it was their first time in Colorado.

title: Norwood school construction raises noise concerns
copy: Construction of Norwood's new school near Pinion Park has drawn noise complaints from neighbors, mostly around early morning and holiday work. The town asks residents to report complaints directly to Town Hall at (970) 327-4288, not the school district. A traffic study also flagged sight-line issues at Grand Ave and South Market St., with crosswalks proposed but parking cuts drawing pushback from trustees.

title: Voting-related measures on November ballots include a voter ID push targeting mail-in ballots
copy: Voters in California, Colorado, and Nevada are deciding on ballot measures this November that would require driver's license or partial Social Security numbers on mail-in ballots. Similar measures appear in Arizona, North Carolina, and Ohio, referred by Republican-led legislatures. Nationally, about 1 in 5 state ballot measures this cycle touch voting rules or election procedures.

title: Spreading humanity through music
copy: Telluride-Boulder indie-folk duo LVDY performed for inmates in a Virginia jail addiction recovery program last April, and a video of the set racked up 4.5 million Instagram views. The pair are now fielding requests from other jail systems and plan to bring live music to more facilities on upcoming tours.

title: Legals and Public Notices for Oct. 22-28, 2026
copy: The Tomboy Lodge Association has filed a foreclosure on Unit 156A at 619 West Columbia Avenue in Telluride over an unpaid HOA balance of $15,449.81. A public auction is scheduled for December 16, 2026, at the San Miguel County Courthouse. A second notice involving The Good Gargoyle Condominiums was also published but cut off.

title: Cynthia Guy
copy: Cynthia "Cindy" Guy, 60, of Colorado passed away September 30, 2026. A massage therapist for over 30 years, she was known for her love of music, dancing, and the natural world. Donations in her memory may be made to Golden Retriever Rescue of the Rockies.

title: Sister of American Stephen Hubbard says he's in disbelief following release by Russia
copy: Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired Michigan teacher held in a Russian prison since 2022, was released Wednesday following a call between President Trump and Putin. His sister says he endured beatings and starvation and now has an enlarged heart. He's headed home, and may settle in Colorado with family.

title: A gathering of ‘people who feel like you do’
copy: A group of Telluride residents has been gathering monthly since January 2025, marching from the San Miguel County Courthouse to Town Park and back. Turnout typically runs a few dozen people, with speakers and occasional sing-alongs. The next march is October 24 at noon.

title: ‘Rings of Time: Tales from the Telluride Bluegrass Festival’
copy: A documentary about the Telluride Bluegrass Festival's 50-year history was pulled from its planned Town Park premiere over concerns about AI-animated sequences, generating unexpected buzz. The film traces the festival's arc from Bill Monroe to Billy Strings, weaving in personal stories including the loss of producer Craig Ferguson's son Griffin. A new release date hasn't been set.

title: Celebrity exorcist priest to take one-year 'media fast' after meeting with Denver archbishop
copy: A prominent Denver-area Catholic exorcist, Fr. Chad Ripperger, is stepping back from public media for a year at his archbishop's request. Ripperger had amassed millions of views online discussing topics like demonic aliens and Tesla. The archdiocese gave no specific reason for the request, which Ripperger accepted.

title: One to One: Yes on 5A
copy: One to One Mentoring's board and staff have come out in support of Ballot Issue 5A, citing concern over funding shortfalls that could affect school programs including Ski PE, Dual Immersion, AP courses, arts, and athletics. The letter is signed by Executive Director Tara Kelley and eight additional staff and board members.

title: 5A is about protecting our values
copy: Ballot Issue 5A is a school funding measure on the local ballot. A community member writes that failing to pass it would mean larger class sizes, fewer opportunities for students, and potential loss of what makes Telluride's schools stand out. The letter urges voters to consider the long-term community impact.

title: Passing 5A is crucial
copy: A local student writes that Ballot Issue 5A matters directly to programs like the Miner School, which lets students earn credit through real work in the community. She's used it to build a career in local restaurants and has been accepted into a hospitality program at Montana State. If 5A fails, Ski PE, AP courses, and work-study programs face cuts.

title: Support our amazing school
copy: A Telluride Middle/High School senior wrote to the editor urging voters to pass Ballot Issue 5A, which would offset a 17% per-student drop in state funding. Without it, the school stands to lose college counseling staff and sports programs. The letter was signed by Ella-Rose Aplin.

title: Does platted density mean anything in town planning?
copy: A letter to the editor raises pointed questions about the Carhenge/Backman Village project after the Sept. 30 Town Council meeting upheld a lot-line vacation. The writer notes the platted density shows 176 units — or 151 plus commercial space — yet planning has advanced a 230-unit proposal, with over $1M reportedly spent on consultants. She's asking what legal weight a recorded plat actually carries if staff can set it aside during project review.

title: Successful school, successful town
copy: Telluride School District is facing a 17% per-student funding cut after Colorado changed its school funding formula, which hit smaller, remote, high cost-of-living districts hard. Ballot Issue 5A would cost a $1M assessed-value homeowner about $117/year; without it, TSD projects losing roughly 55 staff positions and cutting AP, fine arts, and vocational programs.

title: CAFI: Vote sí a la propuesta 5A
copy: CAFI, a local immigrant advocacy group, is urging a yes vote on Measure 5A for the Telluride R-1 School District. They warn that without it, programs like Dual Immersion — where English and Spanish speakers learn side by side — could be cut, along with arts, sports, and college prep. The district says failure could mean losing between 54 and 94 of its 142 staff.

title: Examine facts, evaluate candidates
copy: Sheriff Dan Covault responds to a letter supporting his opponent Lane Masters, citing his 25-plus years in local law enforcement — from corrections to sheriff — versus Masters' fewer than four years as a Colorado peace officer. He addresses disputes over license plate readers, immigration enforcement, due process, and his long-standing unaffiliated voter registration.
letterAuthor: Dan Covault San Miguel County Sheriff

title: Protecting our mountain communities
copy: Telluride's single road in and out makes wildfire risk a constant reality here, and that concern extends across the Western Slope. A letter to the editor highlights Proposition 137, which would direct existing state tax revenues toward forest thinning, prescribed fire, defensible space, and watershed protection — without raising tax rates.

title: CAFI: Vote Yes on 5A
copy: Collaborative Action for Immigrants is urging a yes vote on Ballot Measure 5A for the Telluride R-1 School District. Without it, the district says it could cut 54–94 staff and eliminate programs including Dual Immersion, arts, athletics, and AP courses. The measure would cost roughly $117/year per $1M of residential property value starting in 2027.

title: The tell lies in the cry that 'we cannot compete with Aspen'
copy: Telluride's R-1 School District once ranked #1 in Colorado and top 50 nationally — built through decades of deep community involvement. Now, state and federal funding cuts are putting that foundation at risk, and Ballot Issue 5A is being asked to help bridge the gap. Long-time locals who built those institutions broadly support it.

title: Remembering together
copy: Thrive Community Health Network and Friends of the Telluride Remembrance Garden are dedicating the garden on Oct. 27, 4:30–6 p.m., at the River Trail near Colorado Ave. and Hemlock St. The site received landscaping, native plants, and three new benches over the summer of 2025. The public is welcome.

title: My education in Telluride has been impactful
copy: A Telluride High School senior writes in support of Ballot Issue 5A, describing how district programs — Dual Immersion, AP classes, college prep seminars, arts, and Ski PE — have shaped her path toward pre-med. She notes THS ranks 64th among Colorado's 1,877 public high schools and holds a 1,210 SAT average vs. the state's 994. The levy would cost $117 per year per $1M of assessed home value.

title: Lanterne rouge
copy: The Ophir Pass Hill Climb ran its annual course last October through rain, hail, and sleet — open to cyclists, runners, horses, and dogs, with no horses taking the bait this year. The writer finished last, pushing the bike most of the way up, and caught some friendly grief at the top for it. Been going on long enough that last place still beats not starting.

title: Howard Kornfeld to speak at the library Friday, Oct. 23
copy: Dr. Howard Kornfeld, a former Telluride resident and town consultant who researched local tailings and aquifer risks in the 1980s, returns to speak at Wilkinson Public Library Friday, Oct. 23 at 4:30 p.m. He'll cover his ecological work here alongside topics of world peace and nuclear disarmament. Hosted by Talking Gourds and the library.

title: How Dan Covault earned my trust
copy: A survivor named Lorina writes about how San Miguel County detective Dan Covault reopened a decade-old abuse case after following a single tip, ultimately linking cold cases and securing a conviction. She reported the predator to authorities from 1996–2002 with no result; Covault's 2013 investigation finally brought justice.

title: Death, plants and translocation
copy: As summer's wildflowers brown and drop, they're doing something purposeful — moving sugars and nutrients down into their roots through a process called translocation. Perennials like osha store those reserves underground all winter, then draw on them to push up new growth in spring. Worth knowing if you've ever wondered how it all comes back.

title: Lady Miners hope their recent heat rises
copy: Telluride's varsity volleyball team rattled off five straight wins after a six-match losing streak, including a four-set road victory at Mancos. Standing 9-9 overall and 4-3 in league play, the Lady Miners returned home for three straight home dates, starting with a rematch against Mancos.

title: Yellowstone receives record $105 million gift for infrastructure, conservation, access
copy: Yellowstone National Park is receiving a $105 million private gift — the largest in the park's history — from Tallgrass, a Colorado pipeline and infrastructure company, channeled through a new fund with Yellowstone Forever. A $35 million visitor center at Norris Geyser Basin is among the planned projects. Much of the initiative targets Wyoming students and families.

title: Humbled at home
copy: Telluride's 10-match winning streak ended at home with a 3-1 loss to Coal Ridge. The Miners showed fight late — goalie Maddox Slosberg made several big saves and Ethan Shupp finally got one on the board — but the comeback came too late. Players noted the physical style of play as a useful preview of what playoff opponents will bring.

title: A fond (and family-friendly) farewell to fall
copy: Mountain Village is closing out fall with "Pumpkins & Peaks," a free two-day family event Oct. 24–25 in Heritage Plaza featuring pumpkins, live music, carnival games, a petting zoo, and outdoor football screenings. The gondola stays open a week later than usual this season. Food, drinks, and fall film screenings round it out.

title: The benefits of a bilingual brain
copy: Telluride School's Dual Immersion Program, running since 2014, offers K–8 students half their day in Spanish alongside English. This year, 52% of graduating seniors earned the Colorado Seal of Biliteracy — the program's highest rate yet. Research backs cognitive benefits too, including stronger attention and multitasking skills.

title: Flock defunded: Telluride’s automatic license plate readers turned off
copy: Telluride Town Council voted Oct. 6 to defund its two Flock Safety license plate reader cameras — $5,000/year — cutting short a five-year contract signed in March 2024. The cameras were shut off immediately over privacy concerns tied to reproductive care, immigration status, and potential federal data access. The marshal's department credited the technology with helping solve every major case over the past two-and-a-half years.

title: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. What's their next move?
copy: Latino voters who shifted toward Trump in 2024 are showing signs of buyer's remorse — high gas prices, grocery costs, and ongoing conflict with Iran have soured many who expected economic relief. Competitive House districts in Arizona, Colorado, and Texas with large Hispanic populations are now being watched closely heading into the midterms.

title: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. What's their next move?
copy: Some Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 are now expressing buyer's remorse over gas prices, grocery costs, and ongoing conflict with Iran. AP-NORC polling shows around 6 in 10 Hispanic voters now disapprove of Trump, with over 70% dissatisfied with his economic performance. Arizona's competitive 6th District is one place where that shift could matter come November.

title: Fairway masters
copy: Telluride High School's three-man golf team placed fourth out of 14 schools at the Class 2A State Championship in Pueblo on Oct. 5–6. Sophomore Banks O'Brien tied for third individually, shooting 75-77; sophomore Irvin Ossola tied for 22nd; and senior Gage Wilson, just 18 months into the sport, tied for 43rd. Coach Reinecke called the difficult conditions a motivator heading into next year.

title: A boost for early readers
copy: Telluride R-1's literacy coach Emily Bordogna has secured four years of funding through a Colorado Department of Education Early Literacy Grant, keeping her K-3 coaching position stable despite statewide education budget cuts. A second grant adds a year of outside consulting support. The focus is strengthening core reading instruction so fewer kids need intervention later on.

title: Telluride School District talks housing developments
copy: The Telluride School District is working with Rural Homes and CHFA to expand housing options for employees, with 20 units planned at Two Rivers and additional rentals in Rico and behind the middle/high school. A CHFA program cuts mortgage rates roughly in half — from around 7.7% to 3.5% — with down payment assistance available. The district held information sessions this month so employees could learn about the options and ask questions.

title: THS takes winning ways to Ridgway
copy: Telluride High School beat Ridgway 4-2 on the road, staying unbeaten in league play at 10-1-0. Montano, Clarke (two), and Zago Carolei scored for the Miners, with Young and Slosberg each making nine and seven saves respectively. THS hosts Coal Ridge next Saturday at 11 a.m.

title: A clothing drive with heart
copy: Telluride Storage at 650 S. Park Rd. is running its third annual winter clothing drive through Oct. 27, collecting coats, gloves, hats, boots, and other cold-weather gear via a 24/7 drop box out front. Donated items go to organizations across the region, including Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, and Haven House.

title: Connecting invisible threads
copy: Devaki Murch, a survivor of the 1975 Operation Babylift plane crash, brings her traveling exhibit *My Name is Mimosa* to The Livery in Norwood on Oct. 24 at 7 p.m. She's been reconnecting adoptees, volunteers, and others tied to the airlift using 33 boxes of documents discovered in a nun's basement. Free, open to the public.

title: CHALKBOARD week of Oct. 15-21
copy: The Chalkboard for Oct. 15–21 lists birthdays for 14 locals and runs through recurring community meetings and services in Norwood and the Nucla-Naturita area. Regular fixtures include the Food Pantry, Senior Meals, Free Legal Aid, and pickleball. The Farmers Market runs Thursdays through mid-October.

title: Correction, apology regarding a letter to the editor
copy: The Telluride Times has issued a correction and apology after a letter to the editor incorrectly claimed sheriff's office license-plate-reader accounts were canceled the day before a public records request arrived — the CORA request actually came two days earlier, and account updates were routine policy and personnel maintenance. The paper's own investigation found the allegations unsubstantiated.

title: With anger spreading over Iran war, Democrats hope to flip Republican seats with veterans' help
copy: Democrats are putting money into Colorado's heavily military 5th Congressional District for the first time in years, backing veteran Jessica Killin against Republican Rep. Jeff Crank. Some longtime Republican veterans in the district say the Iran war and Pentagon leadership have them reconsidering their usual vote.

title: Arizona State hires veteran NHL coach Dave Hakstol to lead program, Powers announces resignation
copy: Arizona State hired former NHL head coach Dave Hakstol to lead its hockey program after coach Greg Powers resigned amid an investigation into a workout that left 21-year-old player Matthew Mayich on life support with severe heat stroke. An independent review led by a former state Supreme Court chief justice is ongoing, with findings expected by early December. Hakstol previously coached the Flyers, Kraken, and North Dakota.

title: Everyone has the same question in the midterms — where's the beef? (And how much does it cost?)
copy: Beef has become a recurring campaign theme in this midterm cycle, with candidates in Mississippi, Colorado, Iowa, Texas, and Arizona all fielding attacks or making moves around meat-eating and agricultural policy. Ground beef is running around $6.79 a pound nationally, up from $5.55 in January. Both parties are working the issue, though from different angles.

title: Green Grants program expands to the West End
copy: EcoAction Partners' Green Grants program has expanded into the West End of Montrose County, backed by roughly $85,000 from the Telluride Foundation. Grants typically run $5,000–$10,000 and can go toward heat pumps, windows, and EV infrastructure. The intent-to-apply deadline is October 30 at telluride-co.gosmart.org.

title: We're on the edge of our seats
copy: The Telluride Horror Show runs October 16–18 for its 17th year, with headliners including Universal's upcoming slasher *River* and *Victorian Psycho*. Several films have local ties, including *The Cycle*, which features Telluride's own Jeb Berrier. Free screenings, campfire readings, and library films round out the weekend.

title: Legals and Public Notices for Oct. 15-21, 2026
copy: Sawpit's Board of Trustees will review the town's proposed 2027 budget at a public meeting November 19 at 6:30PM. Separately, a Tomboy Lodge unit at 619 W Columbia Ave is headed to foreclosure sale in San Miguel County, and Good Gargoyle Condominiums mortgage holders are being notified of a proposed declaration amendment.

title: Amendment 83 is a trap, vote No
copy: A Colorado veterinarian of 23 years is urging a No vote on Amendment 83, arguing that while it's framed as protecting hunting and fishing rights — already legal in Colorado — it would enshrine "traditional methods" in the state Constitution. She says supporters have acknowledged this language could revive steel-jawed traps, neck snares, and poisons that voters banned in 1996.

title: 5A prevents devastating cuts
copy: Telluride schools are facing a double financial hit — declining enrollment means less state funding, and Colorado's new formula also cuts per-student dollars. Ballot Issue 5A would use local property taxes to partially offset those state reductions, though per-student funding would still drop even if it passes. Without it, programs like Dual Immersion, sports, and student support services are on the table.

title: Democrat Lane Masters for sheriff
copy: Lane Masters, a Telluride native and Marine veteran, is running for San Miguel County Sheriff as a Democrat. He brings 13 years in law enforcement — including homicide and bomb squad work in Bismarck — plus a degree in emergency management. He opposes ALPRs and ICE cooperation; incumbent Dan supports both.

title: Writing in support of 5A
copy: Telluride R-1's Ballot Issue 5A would raise property taxes roughly $117 per year per $1M assessed value to offset state funding cuts tied to a revised school finance formula. Under the new formula, the district could lose around 17% per-pupil funding — enough to threaten programs. The measure won't close the gap entirely, but would soften the impact.

title: Support continued excellence
copy: Telluride School District ranks in Colorado's top 10% and performs well nationally, but faces a funding squeeze — state per-student funding is down 17% and costs keep climbing. San Miguel County sits near the bottom in Colorado for property tax rates, around half the national average. Ballot Measure 5A would raise those rates to help close the gap.

title: Vote No on Amendment 81
copy: A local resident writes to oppose Amendment 81, which would permanently change the Colorado Constitution to require state and local law enforcement to notify ICE when someone is charged — before any conviction. The writer argues this conflicts with existing state laws limiting ICE authority and raises due process concerns.

title: Ghost Stories
copy: A writer reflects on growing up in an 1820 Maine farmhouse where ghostly figures — a woman in a black hat, a restless child, a man in overalls — were regular presences. The experiences passed to the next generation when her young daughter encountered a spirit at the staircase. The family treated it all as a matter of course.

title: The Times they are a-changin' (again)
copy: The Telluride Daily Planet, bought by Hoffmann Media Group in fall 2025 and renamed The Telluride Times, is now shifting to management under Lee Enterprises, which HMG's owner recently acquired. Starting with the Oct. 29 print edition, readers will notice some layout and sizing changes, though staff, coverage, and familiar features stay the same. The horoscope column is temporarily on hold due to an unrelated subscription issue.

title: Bright sparks
copy: Students at Telluride Middle/High School got a look at the Sparky Scholarship program this week, as board members — including founder Jennie Franks — held their first monthly luncheon of the year. The program, part of True North Youth Program, focuses on academic success and college access. Future applicants are welcome to join upcoming luncheons.

title: October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month
copy: Purple ribbons are going up around the region this month, courtesy of San Miguel Resource Center staff and volunteers marking Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Residents and businesses can call SMRC to get ribbons for their own doors, fences, and windows.

title: I measure return on investment for a living. The math says 'yes' on 5A
copy: Ballot Issue 5A would partially offset a projected $3 million annual drop in state school funding, which the district estimates could eliminate 33–65 positions over five years. The cost to property owners works out to roughly $115 a year per $1 million of assessed value. This guest commentary, written by a local parent and ROI professional, makes the financial case for passing the measure.

title: Good, better, best
copy: The "optimization" trend has saturated daily life — sleep, protein, dopamine, creativity, all of it. Neuroscience is pushing back, showing the brain actually needs boredom and blank space to function well. Worth sitting with before adding whey protein to your soup.

title: Open enrollment is coming
copy: Colorado's Open Enrollment for 2027 health plans runs Nov. 1 through Jan. 15. Enroll by Dec. 15 for Jan. 1 coverage. Thrive Community Health Network offers free, bilingual help — including a local event at Wilkinson Public Library Oct. 15, 4–6 p.m. Call (970) 708-7096.

title: Gondola operating dates extended throughout the next year
copy: The gondola's operating calendar is getting stretched at both ends. This fall it runs through Oct. 25, a week later than usual, and next summer it opens May 20 — also a week early. TMVOA is covering the added costs and pairing the extra days with events.

title: Library hosts talk with author Pam Houston
copy: Pam Houston, author of *Animals Taught Me Everything*, speaks and signs at Wilkinson Public Library Monday, Oct. 26, at 5:30 p.m. The book draws on her experiences with horses, wolves, elephants, and other animals to explore how they model the essentials of living. Houston also wrote *Deep Creek: Finding Hope In The High Country* and lives on a homestead near the Rio Grande headwaters.

title: Chipeta Lodge renews focus on lodging, wellness and community
copy: Chipeta Lodge in Ridgway is refocusing on lodging, spa, and wellness while converting its White Buffalo restaurant into a casual bar with grab-and-go options. Day passes to the pool and spa are now available to locals. Catering for events shifts to Grace & Grit, reviving a partnership from the lodge's 1990s bed-and-breakfast days.

title: A community hub
copy: Kelly and Will Dagostino took over the Sawpit Mercantile in July 2024 and spent their first six months just watching and listening before making changes. They've added espresso, sandwiches, a grab-and-go menu, and free live music while keeping the barbecue program going. When mudslides shut down Highway 145 in July, they kept the doors open, fed stranded travelers until the food ran out, and kept the band playing.

title: County staff discusses housing code updates
copy: San Miguel County held a joint work session to review proposed land use code updates aimed at removing regulatory barriers to housing development, including changes to density rules, new cottage and cohousing definitions, and a 3,000-square-foot cap on free-market homes. Streamlined approval processes would allow smaller projects to move faster through the planning commission.

title: Fairway masters
copy: Three Telluride High School golfers — Banks O'Brien, Irvin Ossola, and Gage Wilson — competed at the Class 2A State Golf Championship in Pueblo on Oct. 5–6, with the team finishing fourth out of 14 schools. Sophomore O'Brien tied for third individually at 10 over par; Ossola tied for 22nd; and Wilson, just 18 months into the sport, tied for 43rd. Coach Reinecke called the result motivating heading into next year.

title: Masters will rebuild sheriff's office
copy: A retired San Miguel County reserve deputy is raising concerns about staffing and morale at the sheriff's office, saying close to half the patrol deputies have resigned since Dan Covault was appointed interim sheriff in June 2025. The letter also questions the timing of license-plate-reader account cancellations the day before a public records request arrived. The writer backs Lane Masters for sheriff in November.
letterAuthor: John Kirkendoll San Miguel County Reserve, Deputy Sheriff (Retired)
